findings.paper_title: Housing Services – Performance, Compliance and Outlook (mid-year)
findings.headline: Recent decline in tenant satisfaction with repair completion timelines, described as 'more marked' than other metrics
findings.detail: Fall in percentage of tenants satisfied with time taken to complete repairs is more significant than declines in other satisfaction indicators. Service being investigated with Mears, the main repairs contractor. Sentiment analysis shows tenants value prompt, high-quality repairs and dissatisfaction results from poor communication, incomplete work, and lack of follow-up.
findings.matters: Service quality decline could affect tenant retention, increase complaints and regulatory scrutiny, and potentially signal underlying contractor performance issues.
findings.figures: 73% of repairs completed in one visit in Q1 improving to 77% in Q2; tenant satisfaction with repair timeliness declining (specific percentage not stated)
findings.quote: The fall in the percentage of tenants satisfied with the time taken to complete repairs is more marked and this aspect of service delivery is currently being investigated with Mears, the main repairs and maintenance contract.

findings.paper_title: Housing Services – Performance, Compliance and Outlook (mid-year)
findings.headline: Potential 4% (£57k) cut to homelessness funding allocation in 2026/27 adds to existing demand pressures
findings.detail: 2026/27 homelessness settlement expected December 2025. Multiple grant streams may be combined, potentially reducing council's allocation by 4% (£57,000). This comes amid rising demand with 1,151 households on housing register (6% increase since March 2025).
findings.matters: Funding cut coinciding with rising homelessness demand creates budget pressure for services the council is already struggling to fund.
findings.figures: Potential £57,000 reduction (4% of allocation); 1,151 households on housing register (6% increase since March 2025)
findings.quote: Funding uncertainties remain, with the 2026/27 local authority homelessness settlement expected in December likely to combine a number of grant streams, potentially reducing the Council's allocation by 4% (£57,000).

findings.paper_title: Housing Services – Performance, Compliance and Outlook (mid-year)
findings.headline: Council projects £720k loss on emergency accommodation budget due to homelessness demand exceeding cost-control target
findings.detail: Number of households in emergency accommodation stands at 253, above the cost reduction target of 219. This overage is explicitly projected to result in a £720k loss against the budgeted figure. Homelessness demand remains high, driven by cost-of-living pressures and 'no fault' evictions.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted £720k loss on a service forecast is material and indicates demand pressures the council cannot control within existing funding.
findings.figures: 253 households in emergency accommodation vs 219 target; £720k projected loss; 692 homeless applications by end Q2
findings.quote: The number is projected to remain above the cost reduction target of 219, and this is projected to result in a loss of £720k compared to the budgeted figure.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council drawing down £643,000 from Flexible Use of Capital Receipts in 2025/26
findings.detail: The capital program shows forecast deployment of £643,000 from Flexible Use of Capital Receipts (a finite, one-off resource). This spending appears unbudgeted originally but has been included in revised budget allocation, indicating either a late-year decision or a reallocation to cover other pressures.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are one-off, finite resources; drawing them down in current year reduces available capacity for future investment or crisis response; repeated use signals structural budget pressure
findings.figures: £643,000 forecast deployment from Flexible Use of Capital Receipts
findings.quote: Flexible Use of Capital Receipts - - - - 643,000 (643,000)

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Smart Technology and Robotics project shows zero spend against £273,000 allocation
findings.detail: A digital transformation project allocated £273,000 (comprising £210,000 carry forward and £63,000 new budget) shows no year-to-date expenditure and zero forecast outturn, indicating the project has not progressed at all.
findings.matters: Non-delivery of digital transformation projects may indicate resource constraints or priority drift; it raises questions about project management capacity and governance
findings.figures: £273,000 total allocation; £0 YTD spend; £0 forecast outturn
findings.quote: Smart Technology and Robotics 210,000 63,000 273,000 - - 273,000

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Motcombe Pool project forecast to overspend its capital budget by £105,802
findings.detail: The Motcombe Pool asset management project has a revised budget of £250,000. Year-to-date spend is £145,802 and the forecast outturn is £355,802, creating an overspend variance of £105,802 (42% above budget). This indicates either scope creep or cost escalation on a locked capital project.
findings.matters: Capital budget overruns reduce available funds for other priorities and may indicate weak project controls or estimation; they signal governance risk to lenders
findings.figures: £250,000 budget; £355,802 forecast outturn; (£105,802) variance

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring - Appendix 1
findings.headline: HRA New Build program forecast to spend only 61% of its £26.4m budget despite significant allocation
findings.detail: The New Build project carries forward £26,387,000 and with no additional original budget, the revised budget is £26,387,000. Year-to-date expenditure is only £3,866,655 (15% of budget) and the forecast outturn is £16,059,228, leaving £10.3m unspent. This represents significant capital slippage on a major housing delivery program.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a headline council priority and major borrowing/partnership commitment; forecast slippage of this scale signals either delivery delays, scope reduction, or capacity constraints that affect financial position and borrowing justification
findings.figures: £26,387,000 budget; £3,866,655 YTD spend; £16,059,228 forecast outturn

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Capital commitments rising sharply: HRA capex planned at £32.5m (2026/27), £35.7m (2027/28), £38.5m (2028/29)
findings.detail: The council's housing capital programme is significantly expanding over the MTFS period. HRA capex is planned at £32.456m in 2026/27, rising to £38.540m in 2028/29—a doubling from recent years (£11.1m in 2024/25). This creates rising debt servicing costs and reduces financial flexibility at a time when the revenue budget is under pressure.
findings.matters: Large, rising capital commitments must be serviced from revenue; combined with EFS dependency and identified budget gaps, this constrains the council's ability to absorb further shocks and increases dependency on borrowing at elevated interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Business rates reset from 2026/27 will reallocate accumulated gains, introducing uncertainty for councils that grew their base
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 includes a business rates reset coinciding with 2026/27, which 'will effectively realign the retained business rates baseline for all councils.' The document notes this 'introduces a degree of uncertainty for councils that have benefitted from significant business rates growth in recent years' and emphasizes it is 'crucial for the council's medium term financial planning to factor in the potential impact of the reset on retained business rates income.'
findings.matters: This is a downside risk materializing in 2026/27 that the council acknowledges but cannot quantify; if Eastbourne's base is cut, it directly widens the identified budget gap.
findings.figures: Effective from 2026/27; accumulated gains since last reset to be redistributed
findings.quote: the reset will effectively realign the retained business rates baseline for all councils. This means that accumulated gains from business rates growth since the last reset will be redistributed, ensuring that allocations better reflect the current economic circumstances and relative needs of each authority. While the reset aims to create a fairer starting point for future funding, it introduces a degree of uncertainty for councils that have benefitted from significant business rates growth in recent years.

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Identified budget gap of £2.1m for 2026/27, rising to £2.274m by 2028/29, with no published closure plan yet
findings.detail: The February 2025 MTFS confirmed a balanced 2025/26 budget only through drawing £2m from earmarked funds. For 2026/27 onwards, a structural budget gap was identified: £2.1m in 2026/27, rising to £2.274m by 2028/29. The interim MTFS acknowledges this gap ('TBC' appears throughout the financial outlook section) but the closure plan remains incomplete pending the Chancellor's December 2025 spending review and Fair Funding Review 2.0 details.
findings.matters: A multi-year identified budget gap of this scale, combined with dependence on unconfirmed government policy outcomes and a half-finished savings programme, creates material delivery risk.
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the MTFS identified a budget gap of £2.1 million, with the shortfall projected to rise to £2.274 million by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Pay inflation assumption revised upward from 2.6% to 3.6% for 2026/27
findings.detail: The February 2025 MTFS assumed 2.6% pay inflation for 2026/27. The interim MTFS now assumes 3.6%, a 40-basis-point increase reflecting 'ongoing national pay negotiations and expected cost pressures.' This revision increases budget pressure and reduces room for manoeuvre.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 40% of council budgets; a single-year upward revision of this magnitude signals that underlying cost assumptions are eroding faster than originally modelled, a pattern that often precedes further reforecasting.
findings.figures: 2.6% (February 2025 assumption); 3.6% (interim MTFS assumption); £563k incremental impact 2026/27
findings.quote: Rate Assumed Feb '25 (%) 2.6% / Rate Assumed Interim MTFS 3.6%

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation crisis continues: 260 households in emergency housing with £773k forecast shortfall in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demand and rising costs for emergency/temporary accommodation, with 260 households currently housed in emergency provision (as of late 2024/25). Q2 2025/26 monitoring identified a net shortfall of £773k for the financial year, 'largely attributable to sustained pressures in housing need and the cost of temporary accommodation.' Nationally, the LGA reports councils face a £260m collective shortfall between housing benefit paid out and DWP reimbursement (a 30% increase in one year).
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is consuming budget and driving EFS need; it is not a headline service cost but a statutory obligation with no local control over demand, making it a structural financial risk.
findings.figures: 260 households in emergency housing; £773k Q2 2025/26 forecast shortfall; £260m national LGA shortfall
findings.quote: During Quarter 2 of the 2025/26 financial year, Eastbourne Borough Council conducted a comprehensive review of its budgetary performance and financial assumptions. The analysis highlighted a forecasted net shortfall of £773,000 for the year-end outturn, largely attributable to sustained pressures in housing need and the cost of temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Interim Medium Term Financial Strategy - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council still dependent on Exceptional Financial Support and planning to transition through £8.1m savings programme
findings.detail: Eastbourne has drawn EFS annually since 2023/24, receiving £2m in 2025/26. The council identifies the strategic finance programme as essential to transition away from EFS, with £6.1m delivered by end-2025/26 and £2m targeted for 2026/27. The CFO notes EFS 'is not considered a viable and sustainable solution' but the transition depends entirely on savings delivery.
findings.matters: EFS reliance signals underlying structural deficits that cannot be fixed by reserves or one-off adjustments; a lender needs confidence the savings programme will actually close the gap.
findings.figures: £8.1m total savings target; £6.1m delivered by end-2025/26; £2m targeted 2026/27; £2m EFS drawn 2025/26
findings.quote: Eastbourne Borough Council required its post Covid Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) in 2023/24, primarily driven by escalating costs associated with providing temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Finance function has recruitment challenges requiring use of agency staff, costing £130,000 in budget pressure.
findings.detail: Corporate Services directorate is facing difficulties recruiting permanent staff in financial services and is filling the gap with agency resources. This creates both cost pressure and continuity risk in a critical function.
findings.matters: Staffing instability in finance is a control risk. Agency reliance is expensive and creates knowledge retention problems. For a lender reviewing financial control, this is a concern.
findings.figures: £130,000 budget pressure from recruitment challenges and agency use
findings.quote: Finance: Recruitment challenges and use of agency staff to support financial services. 130

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA 30-year business plan sustainability remains uncertain due to inflation and rent increase restrictions.
findings.detail: While the HRA shows a £208,000 underspend at Q2, the council explicitly states the long-term sustainability of the 30-year housing business plan 'still has uncertainties due to the impact of recent high levels of inflation and historic Government restrictions on rent increases.' Even with recent government spending review announcements, PWLB rates for housing are still to be confirmed.
findings.matters: Uncertainty around the 30-year HRA plan signals potential future reliance on General Fund support or capital receipts. For a lender, the HRA is a major balance-sheet liability and any question about its viability affects the council's debt sustainability.
findings.figures: £208,000 underspend forecast; £21,000 original budget
findings.quote: Whilst the overall outturn at this early point in the year is positive, it should be noted that the sustainability of the HRA 30-Year Business Plan still has uncertainties due to the impact of recent high levels of inflation and historic Government restrictions on rent increases.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: The Regulator of Social Housing is inspecting the council's compliance with new consumer standards for its housing stock.
findings.detail: The inspection commenced in May 2025. The council is spending £76,600 on consultant support (Inner Circle Consulting phase 2) to address identified compliance gaps and support a wider housing transformation programme. The inspection adds governance risk and potential remediation costs.
findings.matters: Regulatory inspection of a major asset (the housing stock) creates downside risk around compliance costs and potential enforcement action. For a lender, regulatory pressure on the HRA is a governance red flag.
findings.figures: £76,600 phase 2 consultant cost; inspection started May 2025
findings.quote: Shortly after re-appointing ICC, the RSH confirmed in May 2025 that the Council was being inspected.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Council has achieved only 75% of its 2025-26 savings targets as of Q2, relying on contingencies to offset the gap.
findings.detail: With half the year gone, the council has delivered three-quarters of planned savings. It is now using planned contingency budgets (£400,000 remaining as of Q2) to cover the 25% shortfall and other timing variations. Once contingencies are exhausted, there are no further buffers.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls late in the year are expensive and hard to fix. The council is now financing its budget through one-off reserves rather than structural savings, which is not sustainable.
findings.figures: 75% achievement rate; £400,000 contingencies remaining
findings.quote: The Council has achieved 75% of its savings targets for the year so far and is utilising planned contingencies to address remaining pressures.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund deficit has widened by £292,000 in a single quarter, from £481k to £773k.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £773,000 net shortfall as of 30 September 2025, a deterioration of £292,000 compared to Q1. This trend suggests worsening financial position rather than stabilisation, despite the council's mitigation efforts.
findings.matters: A widening deficit signals lost control of expenditure or income. The trajectory matters as much as the absolute figure; this one is moving in the wrong direction.
findings.figures: £773,000 net shortfall; £292,000 increase from Q1 position
findings.quote: As of 30 September 2025, Eastbourne Borough Council is forecasting a net shortfall of £773,000 in the General Fund, an increase of £292,000 compared to the previous quarter.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Emergency and temporary accommodation costs are £768,000 over budget with no expected improvement through year-end.
findings.detail: Eastbourne has 260 households in emergency accommodation, a level that has remained flat since late 2024/25 rather than decreasing as planned. The council projects this will continue through the financial year, creating a £768,000 cost overrun against the £1.1m directorate total. The council says it is 'exploring options for more sustainable housing solutions and enhanced preventative measures' but provides no specifics.
findings.matters: This is the council's single largest budget pressure and shows no resolution pathway. For a lender, uncontrolled homelessness costs are both a drain on reserves and a signal of wider service delivery challenge.
findings.figures: 260 households; £768,000 additional forecast outturn cost; £1.1m Service Delivery directorate total
findings.quote: The number of households in emergency accommodation has remained at about 260 since late 2024/25, rather than decreasing as expected. The Council now projects this will continue through year-end, increasing costs by £768,000.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Customer complaint resolution below target; staffing shortages created backlog, process redesign underway.
findings.detail: Stage 1 resolution is 75% vs 80% target; Stage 2 is 63% vs 80%. The council received 163 stage 1 complaints (37 upheld, 29 partially upheld) and 32 stage 2 complaints (12 upheld, 7 partially upheld). Staffing issues in Customer Experience and Planning First teams created a backlog; a process redesign will shift ownership to service areas in Q2.
findings.matters: Persistent complaint resolution failures and staffing shortages suggest service delivery issues across the council. The uplift rate (37+12 upheld out of 195) indicates substantive service problems that may affect reputation and the council's ability to retain public confidence.
findings.figures: 75% (Stage 1) and 63% (Stage 2) resolution rates vs 80% targets; 163 Stage 1 complaints (37 upheld, 29 partially upheld); 32 Stage 2 complaints (12 upheld, 7 partially upheld)
findings.quote: The Customer Experience team and Planning First have unfortunately both experienced staffing issues meaning there was a period of time when a backlog occurred. A change in process will ensure service areas take ownership for complaints moving forward into quarter 2, joint complaints will be worked on between teams.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Waste container delivery performance collapsed to 64% of target due to 46% demand surge.
findings.detail: Container delivery on-time performance fell to 64.06% in Q1 against a 99% SLA target. A 46% increase in request volume from the prior year and supply lead time constraints prevented the council from maintaining adequate stock. Performance is expected to improve in Q2.
findings.matters: A 46% surge in demand the council cannot meet suggests either capacity constraints or supply chain vulnerability. Service failures may indicate broader resource or asset management issues.
findings.figures: 64.06% achieved vs 99% target; 46% increase in request volumes year-on-year
findings.quote: The considerable decrease is due to large volume of requests and lead times for deliveries, which were up 46% from Q1 last year. We were unable to get stock to keep up with demand this quarter, however we expect performance to improve going into Q2.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Emergency accommodation rising; council exploring leasing and acquisitions to manage costs.
findings.detail: Emergency accommodation stands at 263 households (Q1) vs 258 (Q4), a small increase. The council is exploring initiatives in Q2 including leasing models and working with the development team for acquisitions and new developments to reduce both numbers and costs.
findings.matters: Rising emergency housing is a cost pressure on budgets. The council's pivot toward leasing and acquisition models suggests the pressure cannot be easily resolved and may require significant capital investment.
findings.figures: 263 households in emergency accommodation (Q1) vs 258 (Q4); 22 cases presenting for homeless advice this quarter
findings.quote: In Q2 further exploration into other initiatives will occur, to further reduce the numbers and costs associated with EA including leasing models and working closely with our development team for new acquisitions and development opportunities.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Planned Council Tax Single Person Discount review will temporarily reduce collection performance August through November.
findings.detail: A review starting in July is expected to increase the net collectable debit by approximately £280k longer-term, but will reduce collection performance against target from August through November. Council Tax collection is currently 96.08% against a 97.50% target.
findings.matters: A deliberate policy decision will worsen collection metrics for four months during the financial year; the £280k timing impact must be factored into cash flow and budget planning.
findings.figures: 97.50% target; 96.08% Q1 achieved; £280k expected additional debit; performance impact August-November
findings.quote: A Council Tax Single Person Discount review will commence in July, which is expected to increase the net collectable debit by approximately £280k. This will temporarily reduce collection performance against the target from August through November; however, it will generate additional income in the longer term.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Business Rates collection below target at 97.47% due to economic pressures on businesses.
findings.detail: Collection is 0.03 percentage points below the 97.50% target, attributed to rising National Insurance contributions, higher National Living Wage, and reduction in Retail, Hospitality, and Leisure (RHL) Business Rate Relief. The RHL relief reduction itself increased the net collectable debit by £2m, and the collection gap is narrowing (2.20% to 0.89% June to July).
findings.matters: Named, sustained cost pressures on local businesses signal economic stress that could worsen collection rates. Business rates are a significant revenue source; deteriorating business conditions warrant monitoring.
findings.figures: 97.47% achieved vs 97.50% target; £2m net debit increase from RHL relief reduction; collection gap narrowed from 2.20% (June) to 0.89% (July)
findings.quote: The collection rate is currently below target due to the challenging economic climate, which has impacted businesses' ability to pay business rates. Factors contributing to this include rising National Insurance contributions, higher National Living Wage, and the reduction in Retail, Hospitality, and Leisure (RHL) Business Rate Relief, all of which have added to cost pressures.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Performance - Quarter 1 - 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Housing void re-let times at 102 days more than double the 45-day target.
findings.detail: 19 properties were re-let in Q1, all requiring planned extensive works, taking 102.24 days against a 45-day target. The council attributes the delay to scope of renovations and acknowledges it is implementing process improvements to better coordinate between teams and suppliers.
findings.matters: Extended void periods reduce rental income from housing stock and increase maintenance costs. The significant miss indicates operational issues that may affect the council's ability to manage its housing investment efficiently.
findings.figures: 102.24 days actual vs 45 days target; 19 properties re-let
findings.quote: All 19 properties had planned extensive works impacting the ability to meet the target. Changes to internal processes and systems continue in 2025/2026 to improve communication between teams/suppliers to ensure a more joined up approach.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: Service income is eroding across multiple areas: land charges down 15%, tennis income at risk, and events underperforming.
findings.detail: Land charges income has declined 15% due to reduced search activity. Tennis services face £178k total pressure with £120k relating to tournament income still being negotiated with the LTA. Events also show pressure. This multi-service income erosion suggests either economic weakness among residents and businesses or internal service delivery issues.
findings.matters: Widespread income shortfalls across seemingly unrelated services indicate the council cannot rely on its income budget, either due to economic conditions affecting the borough or internal service quality issues—both are credit concerns.
findings.figures: Land charges down 15%; Tennis £178k pressure; £120k income target for tournaments; Events £55k pressure
findings.quote: Reduction in fee income due to search activity down by 15% - the service is undertaking a review aimed at improving this position.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: The HRA 30-Year Business Plan faces sustained uncertainties from high inflation and government-imposed rent increase restrictions.
findings.detail: While the HRA is currently forecasting a £283k underspend, the council explicitly states that the sustainability of its 30-year housing business plan remains uncertain due to recent high inflation and long-standing government restrictions on rent increases. The outlook is described as continuing to be challenging despite recent government spending announcements.
findings.matters: The HRA's 30-year plan is fundamental to the council's ability to invest in housing and manage its debt; uncertainties here signal the council may face difficult choices between rent increases, maintenance deferral, or capital programme cuts.
findings.figures: £283k underspend at Q1; 30-Year Business Plan
findings.quote: the sustainability of the HRA 30-Year Business Plan still has uncertainties due to the impact of recent high levels of inflation and historic government restrictions on rent increases

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: Grove Road property rental income plans are being abandoned due to Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty, removing £470k of assumed income.
findings.detail: The council previously planned to generate rental income from its Grove Road property but is now reassessing all plans to allow flexibility given possible LGR considerations about the asset's future use. This reassessment is resulting in £470k loss of anticipated rental income, with further details due at Q2. This indicates significant planning uncertainty introduced by the reorganisation.
findings.matters: A council removing £470k of previously planned property income due to organizational uncertainty signals that LGR is creating planning chaos; property assets are typically stable income sources, and their sudden removal indicates material strategic risk.
findings.figures: £470k loss of assumed rental income at Grove Road
findings.quote: previous rental plans are being reassessed to create greater flexibility This is likely to result of £470k loss of assumed rental income

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: External audit costs of £200k are being charged for delayed audit opinions spanning six financial years from 2019/20 to 2024/25.
findings.detail: The council is absorbing £200k in external audit costs related to local audit backstop arrangements and previous years' delayed audit opinions covering six financial years. Finance staffing is additionally pressured by agency costs for supporting the same multi-year accounts work. This multi-year audit backlog suggests potential underlying issues with financial reporting or internal controls.
findings.matters: A six-year audit backlog is a material red flag indicating potential weaknesses in financial reporting, internal controls, or governance capacity that directly affects the reliability of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £200k external audit costs; additional finance agency costs; audit opinions delayed from 2019/20 through 2024/25
findings.quote: £200k of external audit costs relating the local audit backstop arrangements and previous years' delayed audit opinions is expected to be charged to 2025/26 budget.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: Savings plan achievement stands at only 63%, with three significant areas explicitly failing to deliver their targets.
findings.detail: The council has achieved 63% of its planned savings at Q1. Three major projects are explicitly identified as not delivering as planned: bereavement services (£668k shortfall), bus shelter advertising (£200k shortfall), and capital financing (amount unspecified but called significant). The council is using £1.5m contingency reserves to cover the resulting gap.
findings.matters: When a council has achieved only 63% of its savings plan six months in and major projects are failing, it indicates weak spending control and budget management, increasing reliance on one-off funding and reducing financial predictability.
findings.figures: 63% achievement of budget targets; £668k Bereavement Services pressure; £200k Bus Shelter advertising pressure; £1.5m contingency available
findings.quote: This is a significant area where a savings plan is not currently delivering as planned

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Financial Monitoring Report - Quarter 1 2025-26
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs remain at £5m annually with placement numbers stubbornly high and prevention efforts not achieving historical reduction rates.
findings.detail: The council continues to spend approximately £5m every year on temporary accommodation for around 257-262 households. Despite significant prevention activities, placement numbers are not declining as they have in previous years. The service is considering additional approaches including increasing accommodation supply and reducing housing costs, but no clear solution is yet evident.
findings.matters: A council spending £5m on one service with uncontrolled demand and no clear solution is a structural financial risk that directly impacts its credit profile.
findings.figures: £5m every year; 257 households (excluding EHICL placements); 2024/25 yearend 259 households; average 262 households
findings.quote: The largest and most disproportionate pressure faced by the Council continues to be the increased demand and cost of the provision of emergency and temporary accommodation.

news_drafts.headline: Audit finding on Art and Artefacts was risk-accepted rather than remediated despite Minimal assurance
news_drafts.lead: Risk acceptance is a valid control decision but indicates the council is choosing to tolerate unresolved audit findings in this area. It signals prioritization of other work and may indicate constrained audit/management resources.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Position of audits requiring follow-up

news_drafts.headline: Licensing control remediation achieved only Partial assurance as of June 2026, nearly a year after initial audit
news_drafts.lead: Persistent Partial assurance in a compliance-critical area (licensing) suggests either the underlying control gaps are proving difficult to close or progress has stalled. This may indicate service delivery or regulatory risk.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Position of audits requiring follow-up

news_drafts.headline: IT Asset Management controls remain unresolved and are marked in draft status
news_drafts.lead: IT asset controls are foundational to council operations and financial systems. Unresolved weakness in this area may indicate gaps in data security, asset management, or IT governance that affect service continuity and data integrity.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Position of audits requiring follow-up
